title-group.article-title: Efficacy and CNS Toxicity of Nivolumab and Ipilimumab in Rare Cancer Brain Metastases: A Multicenter Basket Trial Analysis (NCI/SWOG S1609)

sec.title: Purpose:
sec.p: To evaluate the efficacy and safety of dual immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICI) in patients with brain metastases (BM) from rare cancers.

sec.title: Patients and Methods:
sec.p: Patients with and without BM received nivolumab (240 mg every 2 weeks) and ipilimumab (1 mg/kg every 6 weeks; NCI/SWOG S1609 DART trial, NCT02834013) across >1,000 sites. Progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS) were estimated using the Kaplan–Meier method; hazard ratios (HR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) were derived from Cox models. Systemic objective response rate (ORR) was assessed by RECIST version 1.1, and adverse events were graded using Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events version 5.0. Intracranial outcomes were assessed in a subset of patients with BM to evaluate the best intracranial response.

sec.title: Results:
sec.p: Among 727 patients, the systemic ORR was 11.5% in those without BM (n = 707) and 10% in those with BM (n = 20; P = 0.76). PFS and OS were similar between groups (PFS: HR = 1.29; 95% CI, 0.81–2.07; P = 0.28; OS: HR = 1.36; 95% CI, 0.81–2.27; P = 0.24). Intracranial response was evaluable in 12 patients with BM (60%). No intracranial complete or partial responses were observed, and six patients (50%) achieved intracranial stable disease as their best intracranial response. Grade ≥3 central nervous system toxicities occurred in 3% of patients without BM and 5% of those with BM (P = 0.43).

sec.title: Conclusions:
sec.p: Dual ICI therapy showed comparable efficacy and safety in patients with and without BM.

boxed-text.p: Brain metastases (BM) are common in advanced malignancies. However, patients with BM are often excluded from clinical trials because of concerns about immune checkpoint inhibitor efficacy and central nervous system (CNS) toxicity. Our national NCI/SWOG S1609 DART trial analysis, the largest for rare malignancies, showed that dual checkpoint blockade with nivolumab and ipilimumab produced similar outcomes in patients with and without BM, without a significant increase in CNS toxicity. These findings support the broader inclusion of patients with BM in future immunotherapy trials to address existing evidence gaps.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Brain metastases (BM) are a common site of distant spread in lung, breast, melanoma, and renal cancers (1), affecting more than 200,000 individuals annually in the United States and are reported in 10% to 30% of all patients with cancer (2). Historically, BM have been managed with surgery, whole-brain radiotherapy, or stereotactic radiosurgery, which provide local control but are limited by tumor heterogeneity and the brain microenvironment (3, 4).

Recent advances have demonstrated the intracranial efficacy of systemic therapies across multiple tumor types, including alectinib in ALK-positive non–small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), which achieved central nervous system (CNS) response rates >80% in the ALEX trial (n = 303; ref. 5); nivolumab–ipilimumab, which produced durable intracranial responses in more than half of patients with melanoma BM (CheckMate 204; n = 94; ref. 6); and tucatinib-based therapy, which improved intracranial outcomes and survival in HER2-positive breast cancer BM (HER2CLIMB; n = 291; ref. 7). Dual use of immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICI) targeting CTLA-4 and PD-1 has shown intracranial efficacy across several malignancies (6, 8, 9). However, their role in BM from rare cancers remains poorly defined due to limited clinical data. Rare cancers, defined by an incidence <6 per 100,000 annually, pose challenges for large trials, resulting in scarce evidence to guide treatment (10, 11).

To address this gap, we conducted a subgroup analysis of the SWOG/NCI S1609 DART basket trial, evaluating the efficacy and safety of dual ICIs in patients with BM from rare cancers compared with those without BM.

sec.title: Study design
sec.p: This analysis utilized data from the SWOG Cancer Research Network trial S1609 [NCT02834013, DART (Dual Anti-CTLA-4 and Anti-PD-1 Blockade in Rare Tumors) trial], a multi-institutional, open-label, single-arm phase II basket study assessing the efficacy of nivolumab (240 mg every 2 weeks) and ipilimumab (1 mg/kg every 6 weeks) in rare cancers. Rare cancers were defined as those with an incidence of six or fewer cases per 100,000 individuals. The trial enrolled patients across 50 histologic baskets, along with three additional groups for PD-L1–amplified tumors, cancers of unknown primary, and other unclassified malignancies.

Enrollment began in 2017 and concluded in March 2023, with more than 1,000 participating clinical sites. Patients with BM at trial enrollment were included in this analysis as a distinct subgroup to evaluate the baseline characteristics, treatment response, progression patterns, and toxicity outcomes.

sec.title: Patient eligibility
sec.p: Eligible patients were ≥18 years old with histologically confirmed rare cancers that had either progressed on at least one prior systemic therapy or had no standard treatment options available to prolong overall survival (OS). Gender was recorded for all participants and included in the analysis. Additional eligibility criteria included an ECOG performance status of 0 to 2, adequate hematologic and organ function, and measurable disease per the RECIST version 1.1 (RRID: SCR_026435). Detailed eligibility requirements have been described in previous publications (12–14).

sec.title: Treatment and monitoring
sec.p: Participants received nivolumab (240 mg intravenously every 2 weeks) and ipilimumab (1 mg/kg intravenously every 6 weeks) until disease progression, unacceptable toxicity, treatment delay exceeding 56 days, or patient withdrawal. Dose modifications were permitted in response to treatment-related toxicities.

The patients underwent clinical evaluations, laboratory assessments, and toxicity monitoring every 6 weeks. Disease response was assessed via imaging at baseline, week 8, week 16, week 24, and every 12 weeks thereafter until progression. Attrition was tracked throughout the study, including reasons for treatment discontinuation such as disease progression, toxicity, or withdrawal. Detailed patterns of progression and discontinuation are reported in Supplementary Table S1.

sec.title: Toxicity assessment
sec.p: Adverse events were graded using the Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events version 5.0 (RRID: SCR_010296) and documented after each 42-day treatment cycle. The highest observed grade per cycle was recorded, along with causality attribution (definitely, probably, or possibly related to treatment or unrelated). Immune-related adverse events were classified as toxicities at least possibly related to treatment.

sec.title: Outcomes and statistical analysis
sec.p: The primary endpoint was the objective response rate (ORR), defined as complete or partial response (CR/PR) per RECIST version 1.1 (RRID: SCR_026435) based on local site assessments. Secondary endpoints included progression-free survival (PFS) and OS, defined as the time from treatment initiation to progression or death and from trial registration to death, respectively. Patients without an event were censored at last follow-up. PFS and OS were estimated using the Kaplan–Meier method, and associations between baseline characteristics and survival were evaluated using Cox proportional hazards models. Multivariable models were adjusted for primary tumor site, age, sex, and performance status, regardless of univariate significance.

Intracranial outcomes were assessed in a subset of patients with BM who had available brain imaging. Analyses included intracranial response rates based on the best intracranial radiographic assessments, rates of intracranial stable disease, progression patterns (intracranial, extracranial, or both), and outcomes stratified by corticosteroid use.
No formal power calculation was performed due to the exploratory study design.

sec.title: Ethical considerations
sec.p: The study was conducted by the SWOG Cancer Research Network, with investigational drugs supplied by the Cancer Therapy Evaluation Program of the NCI through a research agreement with Bristol Myers Squibb. Ethical approval was obtained from SWOG, the NCI, the NCI Central Institutional Review Board, and local ethics committees at all participating sites. All participants provided written informed consent, and the study adhered to the principles outlined in the Declaration of Helsinki.

sec.title: Patient characteristics
sec.p: A total of 727 patients were enrolled, including 707 without BM and 20 with BM. The patient characteristics are summarized in Table 1. The median age was 60 years (range: 18–88) for patients without BM and 55 years (range: 25–82) for those with BM (P = 0.25). Forty-seven percent were male in the cohort without BM compared with 65% in the cohort with BM (P = 0.12). A performance status of 0 was observed in 39% of the patients without BM and in only 10% of those with BM. Patients with BM were more likely to have a performance status of 1 (85%), compared with 54% in those without BM (P = 0.021). Race distribution was similar between groups (P = 0.52), with most patients being White (79% and 80% in those without and with BM, respectively), followed by Black (10% and 5%) and Asian (4% and 10%). Ethnicity was also comparable (P = 0.24), with 92% of patients without BM and 85% of those with BM identifying as non-Hispanic. Among patients without BM, the most common histology was other cancers (33%), gastrointestinal (14%), gynecologic (14%), and head and neck (13%). Among those with BM, the most frequent histologies were other cancers (40%), head and neck cancers (30%), and neuroendocrine tumors (20%). Genitourinary cancer occurred in 9% of patients without BM and 5% of those with BM, whereas lung cancer was present in 5% of both groups. The overall histologic distribution was different between the groups (P = 0.044).

sec.title: Outcomes
sec.p: All 727 patients were evaluable for responses per RECIST version 1.1 (Table 2; Supplementary Fig. S1). The ORR was 10% in patients with BM and 11.5% in those without BM (P = 0.76). A confirmed CR was observed in 2% of patients without BM and in 0% of those with BM, whereas PR occurred in 9% and 10% of patients, respectively. Clinical benefit, defined as stable disease lasting longer than 6 months, was similar between the groups (14% vs. 15%). The rate of clinical benefit (SD > 6 months)/ORR/unconfirmed CR/PR was 28% in patients with BM compared with 25% in those without BM (P = 1). The percentage of patients who experienced disease progression or RECIST failure at the first scan was 64% in those without BM and 70% in those with BM.

sec.p: Kaplan–Meier estimates of PFS and OS stratified by the presence of BM at enrollment are shown in Fig. 1. There was no statistically significant difference in PFS between patients with and without BM in the univariate analysis [hazard ratio (HR), 1.22; 95% confidence interval (CI), 0.77–1.93; P = 0.39] or after adjustment for age, sex, performance status, race, ethnicity, and histology (HR: 1.29; 95% CI, 0.81–2.07; P = 0.28; Fig. 1A; Table 3).

sec.p: Similarly, OS did not significantly differ between the groups in univariate analysis (HR: 1.23; 95% CI, 0.75–2.02; P = 0.41) or after multivariable adjustment (HR: 1.36; 95% CI, 0.81–2.27; P = 0.24; Fig. 1B; Table 3).

sec.title: Progression patterns, treatment responses, and stability in patients with BM
sec.p: In the BM cohort, 16 of 20 patients (80%) had received prior brain-directed radiotherapy. Intracranial progression occurred in seven patients (35%), and extracranial-only progression occurred in 13 patients (65%).

Intracranial response assessment was available in 12 patients (60%). Although no intracranial responses were observed, six (50%) patients achieved stable intracranial disease. Among these, two patients (10% of the total cohort) exhibited prolonged intracranial stability: one with a dysembryoplastic neuroepithelial tumor (1,841 days and ongoing) and one with metaplastic breast cancer (1,094 days, alongside systemic stable disease).

Among the seven patients (35%) with assessment of both intracranial and extracranial target or nontarget sites, four of the seven (57%) showed intracranial stability with concurrent extracranial progression, and two (29%) experienced concurrent intra- and extra-cranial progression. One patient of the seven (14%) experienced intracranial progression despite ongoing systemic response. Specifically, a patient with high-grade neuroendocrine carcinoma developed a new suprasellar mass after achieving a confirmed partial response of 281 days in extracranial disease, indicating discordant progression confined to the CNS. No other patients demonstrated intracranial progression concurrent with systemic response.

sec.title: Steroid use
sec.p: Among the five patients who received corticosteroids before enrollment, three (60%) had intracranial sites that were evaluated, and all three (100%) experienced intracranial progression. In the nonsteroid group (n = 15), 9 of 15 patients (60%) had intracranial sites that were assessed; 6 out of 9 (67%) achieved intracranial stability, and 3 out of 9 (33%) experienced progression. No intracranial CR or PR occurred in either group.

sec.title: Toxicities
sec.p: Treatment-related nervous system toxicities (grade 3 or higher) occurred in 3% of the patients without BM and in 5% of those with BM (P = 0.43; Table 2). Grade 5 treatment-related toxicity was observed in 2% of patients without BM and in 5% of those with BM (P = 0.31), with one patient experiencing fatal paraneoplastic syndrome in cycle 1.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: The S1609 DART study enrolled patients across 53 rare cancer cohorts at more than 1,000 sites (12–15). Our analysis addresses an important evidence gap by evaluating the efficacy and safety of dual ICIs in patients with rare cancers, comparing outcomes between those with and without BM. Systemic efficacy was broadly comparable between the two groups, indicating that clinical benefit is attainable in this historically understudied population.

The overall safety profile mirrored that seen in larger studies of nivolumab–ipilimumab combinations (12–16). In a pooled analysis of 448 patients treated with nivolumab and ipilimumab, treatment-related grade 3/4 adverse events occurred in 55.5% of patients, with 35.7% leading to treatment discontinuation. The most common adverse events of any grade were skin (64.3%) and gastrointestinal (46.7%), whereas grade 3/4 events most frequently involved the liver (17%) and gastrointestinal tract (16.3%; ref. 16). In our study, grade ≥3 treatment-related neurologic toxicities occurred in one patient with BM (5%) and 19 patients without BM (3%), with no unexpected CNS-specific toxicities observed. Grade 5 toxicity was reported in one patient with BM (5%) and 12 patients without BM (2%). CNS-related toxicity remains an important clinical consideration. Our findings support that its toxicity is no different in patients with BM compared with those without.

Our study finds that dual ICI therapy can achieve intracranial disease stabilization in patients with BM. Two patients experienced notably durable intracranial stability: one with a dysembryoplastic neuroepithelial tumor (1,841 days) and another with metaplastic breast cancer (1,094 days). Corticosteroid use and prior brain-directed therapy remain important clinical considerations. All three evaluable steroid-treated patients experienced intracranial progression, whereas six of nine (67%) patients not on steroids maintained intracranial stability. Disease control in this cohort was primarily achieved through stable disease, and intracranial lesions generally remained stable in systemic responders.

Similar anti–PD-1/PD-L1 therapies have been evaluated in patients with BM across tumor types. In melanoma patients with BM, long-term follow-up of the ABC trial demonstrated intracranial responses (51%) and a 7-year OS of 48% with nivolumab plus ipilimumab in untreated, asymptomatic BM (n = 36; ref. 17). In metastatic NSCLC, the CheckMate 227 part 1 trial showed that nivolumab plus ipilimumab improved OS versus chemotherapy in patients with baseline BM (n = 202; HR, 0.63; 95% CI, 0.43–0.92) and demonstrated durable systemic and intracranial disease control (18). Similarly, in renal cell carcinoma with untreated/asymptomatic BM, the CheckMate 920 trial reported a 32% response rate (n = 28) and no new safety signals (19).

It is worth noting that lower ipilimumab doses have been associated with fewer severe adverse events. A meta-analysis showed that nivolumab 1 mg/kg plus ipilimumab 3 mg/kg every 3 weeks caused more grade ≥3 toxicities than the reverse regimen (20). Accordingly, the SWOG S1609 DART trial used nivolumab 240 mg every 2 weeks and ipilimumab 1 mg/kg every 6 weeks to maximize efficacy while minimizing toxicity, especially in patients with BM.

Several biomarkers, such as tumor mutational burden, PD-L1 expression, and microsatellite instability, have been proposed as predictors of responses to ICI. Unfortunately, biomarker data were not uniformly available for our patient cohort, which is a key limitation of this study. Notably, a patient with a high-grade neuroendocrine tumor achieved a confirmed partial response for 281 days, suggesting that additional factors may influence ICI efficacy in rare cancers with BM. Further investigation of predictive biomarkers is warranted to identify patients most likely to benefit from checkpoint inhibition. Our study has several other limitations, including its nonrandomized design, small sample size, and the lack of a centralized imaging review. Moreover, the small number of patients with BM in this clinical trial limits the power and precision of the comparisons. Although we did not observe any statistically significant differences in PFS or OS in this cohort, with N = 20 patients out of 727 having BM, we only had a power of 80% or higher for HR of 2.19 and higher (using Schoenfeld’s formula for power, 80% power, and 5% alpha). For example, the 95% multivariate CI for PFS ranges from 0.81 to 2.07. The upper range of the CI includes HR consistent with clinically significantly worse PFS for patients with BM, whereas the lower end of the interval is consistent with longer PFS in patients with BM. The sample size in this cohort did not allow for a more precise conclusion beyond the full CI of the potential HR.

Our findings provide valuable evidence supporting the potential role of dual ICI therapy in patients with rare cancers and BM. Rates of toxicity and objective response or stable disease did not differ between patients with and without BM. Notably, several patients experienced prolonged clinical benefit, including those with dysembryoplastic neuroepithelial tumor (1,841 days, ongoing), metaplastic breast cancer (1,094 days), esthesioneuroblastoma (336 days), and sarcomatoid lung carcinoma (168 days prior to progression). Overall, this study confirms the clinical benefit of nivolumab combined with low-dose ipilimumab, demonstrating an acceptable safety profile and meaningful antitumor activity in rare cancers with BM.

sec.title: Data Availability
sec.p: SWOG follows all NIH and NCI policies about sharing data. Due to regulatory requirements that vary from trial to trial, SWOG requires review of data requests outside the National Clinical Trials Network (NCTN) Data Archive. The NCTN Data Archive only accepts datasets from phase III trials; because S1609 is not a phase III trial, requests for S1609 data can be made in accordance with the SWOG Cancer Research Network’s Policy 43, which outlines the procedures for data access and required approvals: https://www.swog.org/sites/default/files/docs/2019-12/Policy43_0.pdf. Questions about data requests can be sent to the S1609 trial statistician and co-author, M. Othus, mothus@fredhutch.org.
